796 | 2.4.   General Syntax Principles and Transaction Model
797 | 
798 |    SMTP commands and replies have a rigid syntax. All commands begin
799 |    with a command verb. All replies begin with a three digit numeric
800 |    code. In some commands and replies, arguments are required following
801 |    the verb or reply code. Some commands do not accept arguments (after
802 |    the verb), and some reply codes are followed, sometimes optionally,
803 |    by free form text. In both cases, where text appears, it is
804 |    separated from the verb or reply code by a space character. Complete
805 |    definitions of commands and replies appear in Section 4.
806 | 
807 |    Verbs and argument values (e.g., "TO:" or "to:" in the RCPT command
808 |    and extension name keywords) are not case sensitive, with the sole
809 |    exception in this specification of a mailbox local-part (SMTP
810 |    Extensions may explicitly specify case-sensitive elements). That is,
811 |    a command verb, an argument value other than a mailbox local-part,
812 |    and free form text MAY be encoded in upper case, lower case, or any
813 |    mixture of upper and lower case with no impact on its meaning. The
814 |    local-part of a mailbox MUST BE treated as case sensitive.
815 |    Therefore, SMTP implementations MUST take care to preserve the case
816 |    of mailbox local-parts. In particular, for some hosts, the user
817 |    "smith" is different from the user "Smith". However, exploiting the
818 |    case sensitivity of mailbox local-parts impedes interoperability and
819 |    is discouraged. Mailbox domains follow normal DNS rules and are
820 |    hence not case sensitive.
821 | 
822 |    A few SMTP servers, in violation of this specification (and RFC 821)
823 |    require that command verbs be encoded by clients in upper case.
824 |    Implementations MAY wish to employ this encoding to accommodate those
825 |    servers.
826 | 
827 |    The argument clause consists of a variable-length character string
828 |    ending with the end of the line, i.e., with the character sequence
829 |    <CRLF>. The receiver will take no action until this sequence is
830 |    received.
831 | 
832 |    The syntax for each command is shown with the discussion of that
833 |    command. Common elements and parameters are shown in Section 4.1.2.
834 | 
835 |    Commands and replies are composed of characters from the ASCII
836 |    character set [6]. When the transport service provides an 8-bit byte
837 |    (octet) transmission channel, each 7-bit character is transmitted,
838 |    right justified, in an octet with the high-order bit cleared to zero.
839 |    More specifically, the unextended SMTP service provides 7-bit

901 | 3.1.   Session Initiation
902 | 
903 |    An SMTP session is initiated when a client opens a connection to a
904 |    server and the server responds with an opening message.
905 | 
906 |    SMTP server implementations MAY include identification of their
907 |    software and version information in the connection greeting reply
908 |    after the 220 code, a practice that permits more efficient isolation
909 |    and repair of any problems. Implementations MAY make provision for
910 |    SMTP servers to disable the software and version announcement where
911 |    it causes security concerns. While some systems also identify their
912 |    contact point for mail problems, this is not a substitute for
913 |    maintaining the required "postmaster" address (see Section 4).
914 | 
915 |    The SMTP protocol allows a server to formally reject a mail session
916 |    while still allowing the initial connection as follows: a 554
917 |    response MAY be given in the initial connection opening message
918 |    instead of the 220. A server taking this approach MUST still wait
919 |    for the client to send a QUIT (see Section 4.1.1.10) before closing
920 |    the connection and SHOULD respond to any intervening commands with
921 |    "503 bad sequence of commands". Since an attempt to make an SMTP
922 |    connection to such a system is probably in error, a server returning
923 |    a 554 response on connection opening SHOULD provide enough
924 |    information in the reply text to facilitate debugging of the sending
925 |    system.
926 | 
927 | 3.2.   Client Initiation
928 | 
929 |    Once the server has sent the greeting (welcoming) message and the
930 |    client has received it, the client normally sends the EHLO command to
931 |    the server, indicating the client's identity. In addition to opening
932 |    the session, use of EHLO indicates that the client is able to process
933 |    service extensions and requests that the server provide a list of the
934 |    extensions it supports. Older SMTP systems that are unable to
935 |    support service extensions, and contemporary clients that do not
936 |    require service extensions in the mail session being initiated, MAY
937 |    use HELO instead of EHLO. Servers MUST NOT return the extended EHLO-
938 |    style response to a HELO command. For a particular connection
939 |    attempt, if the server returns a "command not recognized" response to
940 |    EHLO, the client SHOULD be able to fall back and send HELO.
941 | 
942 |    In the EHLO command, the host sending the command identifies itself;
943 |    the command may be interpreted as saying "Hello, I am <domain>" (and,
944 |    in the case of EHLO, "and I support service extension requests").

953 | 3.3.   Mail Transactions
954 | 
955 |    There are three steps to SMTP mail transactions. The transaction
956 |    starts with a MAIL command that gives the sender identification. (In
957 |    general, the MAIL command may be sent only when no mail transaction
958 |    is in progress; see Section 4.1.4.) A series of one or more RCPT
959 |    commands follows, giving the receiver information. Then, a DATA
960 |    command initiates transfer of the mail data and is terminated by the
961 |    "end of mail" data indicator, which also confirms the transaction.
962 | 
963 |    The first step in the procedure is the MAIL command.
964 | 
965 |        MAIL FROM:<reverse-path> [SP <mail-parameters> ] <CRLF>
966 | 
967 |    This command tells the SMTP-receiver that a new mail transaction is
968 |    starting and to reset all its state tables and buffers, including any
969 |    recipients or mail data. The <reverse-path> portion of the first or
970 |    only argument contains the source mailbox (between "<" and ">"
971 |    brackets), which can be used to report errors (see Section 4.2 for a
972 |    discussion of error reporting). If accepted, the SMTP server returns
973 |    a "250 OK" reply. If the mailbox specification is not acceptable for
974 |    some reason, the server MUST return a reply indicating whether the
975 |    failure is permanent (i.e., will occur again if the client tries to
976 |    send the same address again) or temporary (i.e., the address might be
977 |    accepted if the client tries again later). Despite the apparent
978 |    scope of this requirement, there are circumstances in which the
979 |    acceptability of the reverse-path may not be determined until one or
980 |    more forward-paths (in RCPT commands) can be examined. In those
981 |    cases, the server MAY reasonably accept the reverse-path (with a 250
982 |    reply) and then report problems after the forward-paths are received
983 |    and examined. Normally, failures produce 550 or 553 replies.
984 | 
985 |    Historically, the <reverse-path> was permitted to contain more than
986 |    just a mailbox; however, contemporary systems SHOULD NOT use source
987 |    routing (see Appendix C).
988 | 
989 |    The optional <mail-parameters> are associated with negotiated SMTP
990 |    service extensions (see Section 2.2).
991 | 
992 |    The second step in the procedure is the RCPT command.   This step of
993 |    the procedure can be repeated any number of times.
994 | 
995 |        RCPT TO:<forward-path> [ SP <rcpt-parameters> ] <CRLF>
996 | 
997 |    The first or only argument to this command includes a forward-path
998 |    (normally a mailbox and domain, always surrounded by "<" and ">"
999 |    brackets) identifying one recipient. If accepted, the SMTP server
1000 |    returns a "250 OK" reply and stores the forward-path. If the

1305 |    command unless it has actually verified the address. In particular,
1306 |    a server MUST NOT return 250 if all it has done is to verify that the
1307 |    syntax given is valid. In that case, 502 (Command not implemented)
1308 |    or 500 (Syntax error, command unrecognized) SHOULD be returned. As
1309 |    stated elsewhere, implementation (in the sense of actually validating
1310 |    addresses and returning information) of VRFY and EXPN are strongly
1311 |    recommended. Hence, implementations that return 500 or 502 for VRFY
1312 |    are not in full compliance with this specification.

1314 |    There may be circumstances where an address appears to be valid but
1315 |    cannot reasonably be verified in real time, particularly when a
1316 |    server is acting as a mail exchanger for another server or domain.
1317 |    "Apparent validity", in this case, would normally involve at least
1318 |    syntax checking and might involve verification that any domains
1319 |    specified were ones to which the host expected to be able to relay
1320 |    mail. In these situations, reply code 252 SHOULD be returned. These
1321 |    cases parallel the discussion of RCPT verification in Section 2.1.

1323 |    codes 251 and 551 with VRFY (and EXPN) to indicate addresses that are
1324 |    recognized but that would be forwarded or rejected were mail received
1325 |    for them. Implementations generally SHOULD be more aggressive about
1326 |    address verification in the case of VRFY than in the case of RCPT,

1336 | 3.5.4.     Semantics and Applications of EXPN
1337 | 
1338 |    EXPN is often very useful in debugging and understanding problems
1339 |    with mailing lists and multiple-target-address aliases. Some systems
1340 |    have attempted to use source expansion of mailing lists as a means of
1341 |    eliminating duplicates. The propagation of aliasing systems with
1342 |    mail on the Internet for hosts (typically with MX and CNAME DNS
1343 |    records), for mailboxes (various types of local host aliases), and in
1344 |    various proxying arrangements has made it nearly impossible for these
1345 |    strategies to work consistently, and mail systems SHOULD NOT attempt
1346 |    them.

1348 | 3.6.     Relaying and Mail Routing
1349 | 
1350 | 3.6.1.     Source Routes and Relaying
1351 | 
1352 |    In general, the availability of Mail eXchanger records in the domain
1353 |    name system (RFC 1035 [2], RFC 974 [12]) makes the use of explicit
1354 |    source routes in the Internet mail system unnecessary. Many
1355 |    historical problems with the interpretation of explicit source routes
1356 |    have made their use undesirable. SMTP clients SHOULD NOT generate
1357 |    explicit source routes except under unusual circumstances. SMTP
1358 |    servers MAY decline to act as mail relays or to accept addresses that
1359 |    specify source routes. When route information is encountered, SMTP
1360 |    servers MAY ignore the route information and simply send to the final
1361 |    destination specified as the last element in the route and SHOULD do
1362 |    so. There has been an invalid practice of using names that do not
1363 |    appear in the DNS as destination names, with the senders counting on
1364 |    the intermediate hosts specified in source routing to resolve any
1365 |    problems. If source routes are stripped, this practice will cause
1366 |    failures. This is one of several reasons why SMTP clients MUST NOT
1367 |    generate invalid source routes or depend on serial resolution of
1368 |    names.
1369 | 
1370 |    When source routes are not used, the process described in RFC 821 for
1371 |    constructing a reverse-path from the forward-path is not applicable
1372 |    and the reverse-path at the time of delivery will simply be the
1373 |    address that appeared in the MAIL command.
1374 | 
1375 | 3.6.2.     Mail eXchange Records and Relaying
1376 | 
1377 |    A relay SMTP server is usually the target of a DNS MX record that
1378 |    designates it, rather than the final delivery system. The relay
1379 |    server may accept or reject the task of relaying the mail in the same
1380 |    way it accepts or rejects mail for a local user. If it accepts the
1381 |    task, it then becomes an SMTP client, establishes a transmission
1382 |    channel to the next SMTP server specified in the DNS (according to
1383 |    the rules in Section 5), and sends it the mail. If it declines to

1392 |    SHOULD be returned.

1394 |    This specification does not deal with the verification of return
1395 |    paths for use in delivery notifications. Recent work, such as that
1396 |    on SPF [29] and DKIM [30] [31], has been done to provide ways to

1399 |    path before using its address for delivery notifications, but methods
1400 |    of doing so are not defined here nor is any particular method

1403 | 3.6.3.     Message Submission Servers as Relays
1404 | 
1405 |    Many mail-sending clients exist, especially in conjunction with
1406 |    facilities that receive mail via POP3 or IMAP, that have limited
1407 |    capability to support some of the requirements of this specification,
1408 |    such as the ability to queue messages for subsequent delivery
1409 |    attempts. For these clients, it is common practice to make private
1410 |    arrangements to send all messages to a single server for processing
1411 |    and subsequent distribution. SMTP, as specified here, is not ideally
1412 |    suited for this role. A standardized mail submission protocol has
1413 |    been developed that is gradually superseding practices based on SMTP
1414 |    (see RFC 4409 [18]). In any event, because these arrangements are
1415 |    private and fall outside the scope of this specification, they are
1416 |    not described here.
1417 | 
1418 |    It is important to note that MX records can point to SMTP servers
1419 |    that act as gateways into other environments, not just SMTP relays
1420 |    and final delivery systems; see Sections 3.7 and 5.
1421 | 
1422 |    If an SMTP server has accepted the task of relaying the mail and
1423 |    later finds that the destination is incorrect or that the mail cannot
1424 |    be delivered for some other reason, then it MUST construct an
1425 |    "undeliverable mail" notification message and send it to the
1426 |    originator of the undeliverable mail (as indicated by the reverse-
1427 |    path). Formats specified for non-delivery reports by other standards
1428 |    (see, for example, RFC 3461 [32] and RFC 3464 [33]) SHOULD be used if
1429 |    possible.
1430 | 
1431 |    This notification message must be from the SMTP server at the relay
1432 |    host or the host that first determines that delivery cannot be
1433 |    accomplished. Of course, SMTP servers MUST NOT send notification
1434 |    messages about problems transporting notification messages. One way
1435 |    to prevent loops in error reporting is to specify a null reverse-path
1436 |    in the MAIL command of a notification message. When such a message
1437 |    is transmitted, the reverse-path MUST be set to null (see

1458 | 3.7.     Mail Gatewaying
1459 | 
1460 |    While the relay function discussed above operates within the Internet
1461 |    SMTP transport service environment, MX records or various forms of
1462 |    explicit routing may require that an intermediate SMTP server perform
1463 |    a translation function between one transport service and another. As
1464 |    discussed in Section 2.3.10, when such a system is at the boundary
1465 |    between two transport service environments, we refer to it as a
1466 |    "gateway" or "gateway SMTP".
1467 | 
1468 |    Gatewaying mail between different mail environments, such as
1469 |    different mail formats and protocols, is complex and does not easily
1470 |    yield to standardization. However, some general requirements may be
1471 |    given for a gateway between the Internet and another mail
1472 |    environment.
1473 | 
1474 | 3.7.1.     Header Fields in Gatewaying
1475 | 
1476 |    Header fields MAY be rewritten when necessary as messages are
1477 |    gatewayed across mail environment boundaries. This may involve
1478 |    inspecting the message body or interpreting the local-part of the
1479 |    destination address in spite of the prohibitions in Section 6.4.
1480 | 
1481 |    Other mail systems gatewayed to the Internet often use a subset of
1482 |    the RFC 822 header section or provide similar functionality with a
1483 |    different syntax, but some of these mail systems do not have an
1484 |    equivalent to the SMTP envelope. Therefore, when a message leaves
1485 |    the Internet environment, it may be necessary to fold the SMTP
1486 |    envelope information into the message header section. A possible
1487 |    solution would be to create new header fields to carry the envelope
1488 |    information (e.g., "X-SMTP-MAIL:" and "X-SMTP-RCPT:"); however, this
1489 |    would require changes in mail programs in foreign environments and
1490 |    might risk disclosure of private information (see Section 7.2).

1499 | 3.7.2.     Received Lines in Gatewaying
1500 | 
1501 |    When forwarding a message into or out of the Internet environment, a
1502 |    gateway MUST prepend a Received: line, but it MUST NOT alter in any
1503 |    way a Received: line that is already in the header section.
1504 | 
1505 |    "Received:" header fields of messages originating from other
1506 |    environments may not conform exactly to this specification. However,
1507 |    the most important use of Received: lines is for debugging mail
1508 |    faults, and this debugging can be severely hampered by well-meaning
1509 |    gateways that try to "fix" a Received: line. As another consequence
1510 |    of trace header fields arising in non-SMTP environments, receiving
1511 |    systems MUST NOT reject mail based on the format of a trace header
1512 |    field and SHOULD be extremely robust in the light of unexpected
1513 |    information or formats in those header fields.
1514 | 
1515 |    The gateway SHOULD indicate the environment and protocol in the "via"
1516 |    clauses of Received header field(s) that it supplies.
1517 | 
1518 | 3.7.3.     Addresses in Gatewaying
1519 | 
1520 |    From the Internet side, the gateway SHOULD accept all valid address
1521 |    formats in SMTP commands and in the RFC 822 header section, and all
1522 |    valid RFC 822 messages. Addresses and header fields generated by
1523 |    gateways MUST conform to applicable standards (including this one and
1524 |    RFC 5322 [4]). Gateways are, of course, subject to the same rules
1525 |    for handling source routes as those described for other SMTP systems
1526 |    in Section 3.3.
1527 | 
1528 | 3.7.4.     Other Header Fields in Gatewaying
1529 | 
1530 |    The gateway MUST ensure that all header fields of a message that it
1531 |    forwards into the Internet mail environment meet the requirements for
1532 |    Internet mail. In particular, all addresses in "From:", "To:",
1533 |    "Cc:", etc., header fields MUST be transformed (if necessary) to
1534 |    satisfy the standard header syntax of RFC 5322 [4], MUST reference
1535 |    only fully-qualified domain names, and MUST be effective and useful
1536 |    for sending replies. The translation algorithm used to convert mail
1537 |    from the Internet protocols to another environment's protocol SHOULD
1538 |    ensure that error messages from the foreign mail environment are
1539 |    delivered to the reverse-path from the SMTP envelope, not to an
1540 |    address in the "From:", "Sender:", or similar header fields of the
1541 |    message.

1559 | 3.8.     Terminating Sessions and Connections
1560 | 
1561 |    An SMTP connection is terminated when the client sends a QUIT
1562 |    command. The server responds with a positive reply code, after which
1563 |    it closes the connection.
1564 | 
1565 |    An SMTP server MUST NOT intentionally close the connection under
1566 |    normal operational circumstances (see Section 7.8) except:
1567 | 
1568 |    o     After receiving a QUIT command and responding with a 221 reply.
1569 | 
1570 |    o     After detecting the need to shut down the SMTP service and
1571 |          returning a 421 response code. This response code can be issued
1572 |          after the server receives any command or, if necessary,
1573 |          asynchronously from command receipt (on the assumption that the
1574 |          client will receive it after the next command is issued).
1575 | 
1576 |    o     After a timeout, as specified in Section 4.5.3.2, occurs waiting
1577 |          for the client to send a command or data.
1578 | 
1579 |    In particular, a server that closes connections in response to
1580 |    commands that are not understood is in violation of this
1581 |    specification. Servers are expected to be tolerant of unknown
1582 |    commands, issuing a 500 reply and awaiting further instructions from
1583 |    the client.
1584 | 
1585 |    An SMTP server that is forcibly shut down via external means SHOULD
1586 |    attempt to send a line containing a 421 response code to the SMTP
1587 |    client before exiting. The SMTP client will normally read the 421
1588 |    response code after sending its next command.
1589 | 
1590 |    SMTP clients that experience a connection close, reset, or other
1591 |    communications failure due to circumstances not under their control
1592 |    (in violation of the intent of this specification but sometimes
1593 |    unavoidable) SHOULD, to maintain the robustness of the mail system,
1594 |    treat the mail transaction as if a 451 response had been received and
1595 |    act accordingly.

1604 | 3.9.     Mailing Lists and Aliases
1605 | 
1606 |    An SMTP-capable host SHOULD support both the alias and the list
1607 |    models of address expansion for multiple delivery. When a message is
1608 |    delivered or forwarded to each address of an expanded list form, the
1609 |    return address in the envelope ("MAIL FROM:") MUST be changed to be
1610 |    the address of a person or other entity who administers the list.
1611 |    However, in this case, the message header section (RFC 5322 [4]) MUST
1612 |    be left unchanged; in particular, the "From" field of the header
1613 |    section is unaffected.
1614 | 
1615 |    An important mail facility is a mechanism for multi-destination
1616 |    delivery of a single message, by transforming (or "expanding" or
1617 |    "exploding") a pseudo-mailbox address into a list of destination
1618 |    mailbox addresses. When a message is sent to such a pseudo-mailbox
1619 |    (sometimes called an "exploder"), copies are forwarded or
1620 |    redistributed to each mailbox in the expanded list. Servers SHOULD
1621 |    simply utilize the addresses on the list; application of heuristics
1622 |    or other matching rules to eliminate some addresses, such as that of
1623 |    the originator, is strongly discouraged. We classify such a pseudo-
1624 |    mailbox as an "alias" or a "list", depending upon the expansion
1625 |    rules.
1626 | 
1627 | 3.9.1.     Alias
1628 | 
1629 |    To expand an alias, the recipient mailer simply replaces the pseudo-
1630 |    mailbox address in the envelope with each of the expanded addresses
1631 |    in turn; the rest of the envelope and the message body are left
1632 |    unchanged. The message is then delivered or forwarded to each
1633 |    expanded address.
1634 | 
1635 | 3.9.2.     List
1636 | 
1637 |    A mailing list may be said to operate by "redistribution" rather than
1638 |    by "forwarding". To expand a list, the recipient mailer replaces the
1639 |    pseudo-mailbox address in the envelope with each of the expanded
1640 |    addresses in turn. The return (backward-pointing) address in the
1641 |    envelope is changed so that all error messages generated by the final
1642 |    deliveries will be returned to a list administrator, not to the
1643 |    message originator, who generally has no control over the contents of
1644 |    the list and will typically find error messages annoying. Note that
1645 |    the key difference between handling aliases (Section 3.9.1) and
1646 |    forwarding (this subsection) is the change to the backward-pointing
1647 |    address in this case. When a list constrains its processing to the
1648 |    very limited set of modifications and actions described here, it is
1649 |    attempting to emulate an MTA; such lists can be treated as a
1650 |    continuation in email transit.
1651 |

1660 |      extensive, modifications to a message and its envelope. Such mailing
1661 |      lists need to be viewed as full MUAs, which accept a delivery and

1668 | 4.1.1.     Command Semantics and Syntax
1669 | 
1670 |      The SMTP commands define the mail transfer or the mail system
1671 |      function requested by the user. SMTP commands are character strings
1672 |      terminated by <CRLF>. The commands themselves are alphabetic
1673 |      characters terminated by <SP> if parameters follow and <CRLF>
1674 |      otherwise. (In the interest of improved interoperability, SMTP
1675 |      receivers SHOULD tolerate trailing white space before the terminating
1676 |      <CRLF>.) The syntax of the local part of a mailbox MUST conform to
1677 |      receiver site conventions and the syntax specified in Section 4.1.2.
1678 |      The SMTP commands are discussed below. The SMTP replies are
1679 |      discussed in Section 4.2.
1680 | 
1681 |      A mail transaction involves several data objects that are
1682 |      communicated as arguments to different commands. The reverse-path is
1683 |      the argument of the MAIL command, the forward-path is the argument of
1684 |      the RCPT command, and the mail data is the argument of the DATA
1685 |      command. These arguments or data objects must be transmitted and
1686 |      held, pending the confirmation communicated by the end of mail data
1687 |      indication that finalizes the transaction. The model for this is
1688 |      that distinct buffers are provided to hold the types of data objects;
1689 |      that is, there is a reverse-path buffer, a forward-path buffer, and a
1690 |      mail data buffer. Specific commands cause information to be appended
1691 |      to a specific buffer, or cause one or more buffers to be cleared.
1692 | 
1693 |      Several commands (RSET, DATA, QUIT) are specified as not permitting
1694 |      parameters. In the absence of specific extensions offered by the
1695 |      server and accepted by the client, clients MUST NOT send such
1696 |      parameters and servers SHOULD reject commands containing them as
1697 |      having invalid syntax.

1902 | 
1903 |    The receiver normally sends a 354 response to DATA, and then treats
1904 |    the lines (strings ending in <CRLF> sequences, as described in
1905 |    Section 2.3.7) following the command as mail data from the sender.
1906 |    This command causes the mail data to be appended to the mail data
1907 |    buffer. The mail data may contain any of the 128 ASCII character
1908 |    codes, although experience has indicated that use of control
1909 |    characters other than SP, HT, CR, and LF may cause problems and

1913 |    is, the character sequence "<CRLF>.<CRLF>", where the first <CRLF> is
1914 |    actually the terminator of the previous line (see Section 4.5.2).
1915 |    This is the end of mail data indication. The first <CRLF> of this
1916 |    terminating sequence is also the <CRLF> that ends the final line of
1917 |    the data (message text) or, if there was no mail data, ends the DATA

1920 |    fields required by this specification nor the message header section

2329 |    it is issued after the session begins and the EHLO command is
2330 |    acceptable to the SMTP server, the SMTP server MUST clear all buffers

2419 | 4.2.     SMTP Replies
2420 | 
2421 |    Replies to SMTP commands serve to ensure the synchronization of
2422 |    requests and actions in the process of mail transfer and to guarantee
2423 |    that the SMTP client always knows the state of the SMTP server.
2424 |    Every command MUST generate exactly one reply.

2426 |    The details of the command-reply sequence are described in
2427 |    Section 4.3.

2429 |    An SMTP reply consists of a three digit number (transmitted as three
2430 |    numeric characters) followed by some text unless specified otherwise
2431 |    in this document. The number is for use by automata to determine
2432 |    what state to enter next; the text is for the human user. The three
2433 |    digits contain enough encoded information that the SMTP client need
2434 |    not examine the text and may either discard it or pass it on to the

2436 |    document. In particular, the 220, 221, 251, 421, and 551 reply codes
2437 |    are associated with message text that must be parsed and interpreted

2439 |    and context dependent, so there are likely to be varying texts for
2440 |    each reply code. A discussion of the theory of reply codes is given
2441 |    in Section 4.2.1. Formally, a reply is defined to be the sequence: a
2442 |    three-digit code, <SP>, one line of text, and <CRLF>, or a multiline
2443 |    reply (as defined in the same section). Since, in violation of this
2444 |    specification, the text is sometimes not sent, clients that do not

# Email Validation Rules

Extracted from RFC 5321 (SMTP) and RFC 5322 (Internet Message Format).

---

## R1 — Address structure: exactly one `@`
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`addr-spec = local-part "@" domain`  
A valid email address MUST contain exactly one `@` character separating the local-part from the domain.

## R2 — Local-part maximum length: 64 octets
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.1  
The maximum total length of a user name or other local-part is **64 octets**.

## R3 — Domain maximum length: 255 octets
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.2  
The maximum total length of a domain name or number is **255 octets**.

## R4 — Local-part dot-atom form: allowed characters
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3, §3.4.1  
`atext = ALPHA / DIGIT / "!" / "#" / "$" / "%" / "&" / "'" / "*" / "+" / "-" / "/" / "=" / "?" / "^" / "_" / "`" / "{" / "|" / "}" / "~"`  
`dot-atom-text = 1*atext *("." 1*atext)`  
In dot-atom form the local-part consists of `atext` characters optionally separated by dots. The characters `(`, `)`, `<`, `>`, `[`, `]`, `:`, `;`, `@`, `\`, `,`, and `"` (specials) are NOT allowed in the dot-atom form.

## R5 — Local-part dot rules: no leading, trailing, or consecutive dots
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3, §3.4.1  
`dot-atom-text = 1*atext *("." 1*atext)`  
In dot-atom form, the local-part must NOT begin with a dot, end with a dot, or contain consecutive dots (`..`).

## R6 — Local-part quoted-string form
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.4, §3.4.1 / RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
The local-part MAY be a quoted-string enclosed in double-quote characters (`"`). Inside the quoted string, any printable ASCII character (except `"` and `\`) is allowed without escaping; `"` and `\` must be escaped as `\"` and `\\`.  
RFC 5321 qtextSMTP: `%d32-33 / %d35-91 / %d93-126` (space and printable US-ASCII except `"` and `\`).

## R7 — Domain dot-atom form: sub-domain labels
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
`Domain = sub-domain *("." sub-domain)`  
`sub-domain = Let-dig [Ldh-str]`  
`Let-dig = ALPHA / DIGIT`  
`Ldh-str = *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" ) Let-dig`  
Each label must start with a letter or digit, end with a letter or digit, and contain only letters, digits, and hyphens. Underscores and other special characters are NOT permitted in domain labels.

## R8 — Domain label: no leading or trailing hyphen
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
`sub-domain = Let-dig [Ldh-str]` and `Ldh-str = *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" ) Let-dig`  
Domain labels MUST NOT begin or end with a hyphen.

## R9 — Domain: at least one dot for FQDN (internet mail)
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.3.5  
Only resolvable, fully-qualified domain names (FQDNs) are permitted in SMTP; a single-label domain (no dot) is not a valid FQDN on the public Internet (exception: the `simple_host` option relaxes this for local contexts).

## R10 — Domain literal: IPv4 address in brackets
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.3 / RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`address-literal = "[" ( IPv4-address-literal / IPv6-address-literal / General-address-literal ) "]"`  
When the domain part is an IP address literal it MUST be enclosed in square brackets `[...]`. For IPv4: `[d.d.d.d]` where each octet is 0–255.

## R11 — Domain literal: IPv6 address in brackets with `IPv6:` tag
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.3  
`IPv6-address-literal = "IPv6:" IPv6-addr`  
IPv6 literals MUST use the `IPv6:` prefix inside brackets, e.g., `[IPv6:::1]`.

## R12 — Local-part case sensitivity
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.4  
The local-part of a mailbox MUST BE treated as case-sensitive by SMTP servers. (The validators library accepts both cases as syntactically valid.)

## R13 — Domain case insensitivity
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.4  
Mailbox domains follow normal DNS rules and are hence NOT case-sensitive.

## R14 — No bare `@` — both parts required
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1 / RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
Both the local-part and the domain part MUST be non-empty.

## R15 — Local-part specials not allowed outside quoted-string
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3  
`specials = "(" / ")" / "<" / ">" / "[" / "]" / ":" / ";" / "@" / "\" / "," / "." / DQUOTE`  
These characters appear in `specials` (not in `atext`) and MUST NOT appear in an unquoted local-part.

## R16 — Space not allowed in unquoted local-part
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3  
Whitespace (SP, HTAB) is not in `atext` and therefore MUST NOT appear in an unquoted local-part or outside CFWS context.

## R17 — Domain must not be empty
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`addr-spec = local-part "@" domain` requires a non-empty domain portion.

## R18 — Local-part must not be empty
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`local-part = dot-atom / quoted-string / obs-local-part` requires at least one character.

## R19 — atext characters are case-insensitive for matching
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3  
Both upper-case and lower-case letters are `ALPHA` and therefore valid atext. The local-part alphabet includes A–Z and a–z.

## R20 — Non-ASCII (high-bit) characters NOT permitted in standard SMTP
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.4  
Systems MUST NOT define mailboxes that require non-ASCII characters (octets with the high-order bit set) in SMTP. The unextended SMTP service is 7-bit only.  
*(The validators library uses the `@validator` decorator and does accept certain extended Latin characters as an implementation extension; tests for that rely on the implementation docstring.)*

"""Spec tests for email local-part rules.

Rules covered: R1, R2, R4, R5, R12, R14, R15, R16, R18, R19
Sources: RFC 5322 §3.2.3, §3.4.1 / RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.1, §4.1.2, §2.4
"""

import validators


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R1 — exactly one @ sign
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_no_at_sign_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.4.1 — R1

    addr-spec requires exactly one '@'. An address with no '@' is invalid.
    """
    assert not validators.email("userwithoutatsign.com")


def test_two_at_signs_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.4.1 — R1

    addr-spec requires exactly one '@'. Two '@' signs are invalid.
    """
    assert not validators.email("user@@example.com")


def test_single_at_sign_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.4.1 — R1

    A properly formed addr-spec with exactly one '@' is valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("user@example.com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R2 — local-part max 64 octets
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_local_part_exactly_64_chars_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.5.3.1.1 — R2

    Local-part of exactly 64 characters (the maximum) MUST be accepted.
    """
    local = "a" * 64
    assert validators.email(f"{local}@example.com")


def test_local_part_65_chars_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.5.3.1.1 — R2

    Local-part exceeding 64 octets MUST be rejected.
    """
    local = "a" * 65
    assert not validators.email(f"{local}@example.com")


def test_local_part_1_char_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.5.3.1.1 — R2

    A single-character local-part is within the 64-octet limit and is valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("a@example.com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R4 — dot-atom atext characters
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_local_part_all_atext_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R4

    All atext characters are valid in an unquoted local-part.
    atext = ALPHA / DIGIT / ! # $ % & ' * + - / = ? ^ _ ` { | } ~
    """
    assert validators.email("a1!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-z@example.com")


def test_local_part_digits_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R4

    Digits are valid atext characters in the local-part.
    """
    assert validators.email("123@example.com")


def test_local_part_mixed_alpha_digit_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R4

    Mixed alphanumeric local-parts are valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("user123@example.com")


def test_local_part_uppercase_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R19

    Uppercase letters are valid atext characters (ALPHA includes A-Z).
    """
    assert validators.email("User@example.com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R5 — no leading, trailing, or consecutive dots
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_local_part_dot_in_middle_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R5

    Dots are allowed in the middle of the local-part (dot-atom form).
    """
    assert validators.email("first.last@example.com")


def test_local_part_leading_dot_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R5

    dot-atom-text requires 1*atext before any dot; a leading dot is invalid.
    """
    assert not validators.email(".user@example.com")


def test_local_part_trailing_dot_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R5

    dot-atom-text requires 1*atext after each dot; a trailing dot is invalid.
    """
    assert not validators.email("user.@example.com")


def test_local_part_consecutive_dots_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R5

    Two consecutive dots in the local-part are invalid in dot-atom form
    because each dot must be surrounded by 1*atext on both sides.
    """
    assert not validators.email("us..er@example.com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R14 / R18 — non-empty local-part and non-empty domain
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_empty_local_part_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.4.1 — R14, R18

    An empty local-part (bare '@domain') is invalid.
    """
    assert not validators.email("@example.com")


def test_empty_string_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.4.1 — R14

    An empty string has no '@' and is invalid.
    """
    assert not validators.email("")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R15 — specials not allowed outside quoted-string
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_local_part_parenthesis_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R15

    '(' and ')' are 'specials', not 'atext', so they are invalid in an
    unquoted local-part.
    """
    assert not validators.email("us(er@example.com")


def test_local_part_angle_bracket_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R15

    '<' is a 'special', not 'atext', so it is invalid in an unquoted
    local-part.
    """
    assert not validators.email("us<er@example.com")


def test_local_part_comma_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R15

    ',' is a 'special', not 'atext', so it is invalid in an unquoted
    local-part.
    """
    assert not validators.email("us,er@example.com")


def test_local_part_colon_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R15

    ':' is a 'special', not 'atext', so it is invalid in an unquoted
    local-part.
    """
    assert not validators.email("us:er@example.com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R16 — no whitespace in unquoted local-part
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_local_part_space_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R16

    Space (SP) is not an atext character and must not appear in an unquoted
    local-part.
    """
    assert not validators.email("us er@example.com")

"""Spec tests for email domain part rules.

Rules covered: R3, R7, R8, R9, R13, R17
Sources: RFC 5321 §4.1.2, §4.5.3.1.2, §2.3.5 / RFC 5322 §3.4.1
"""

import validators


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R3 — domain max 253/255 octets
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_domain_253_chars_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.5.3.1.2 — R3

    The maximum domain length is 255 octets per RFC 5321. The implementation
    checks <= 253 (consistent with DNS name constraints). A 253-character
    domain is valid.
    """
    # 63-char label + dot + 63-char label + dot + 63-char label + dot + 63-char TLD
    # = 63+1+63+1+63+1+61 = 253 chars total
    label_a = "a" * 63
    label_b = "b" * 63
    label_c = "c" * 63
    label_d = "d" * 61
    domain = f"{label_a}.{label_b}.{label_c}.{label_d}"
    assert len(domain) == 253
    assert validators.email(f"user@{domain}")


def test_domain_exceeds_253_chars_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.5.3.1.2 — R3

    A domain exceeding 253 characters is invalid.
    """
    # 254-character domain
    label = "a" * 63
    domain = f"{label}.{label}.{label}." + "b" * 62
    assert len(domain) == 254
    assert not validators.email(f"user@{domain}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R7 — sub-domain labels: letters, digits, hyphens only
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_domain_letters_only_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R7

    Domain labels composed solely of letters are valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("user@example.com")


def test_domain_letters_and_digits_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R7

    Domain labels with letters and digits are valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("user@example2.com")


def test_domain_with_hyphen_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R7

    Hyphens are allowed within domain labels (not at start/end).
    """
    assert validators.email("user@my-host.example.com")


def test_domain_label_underscore_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R7

    RFC 5321 §4.1.2 explicitly states that underscores MUST NOT appear in
    domain name labels for SMTP.
    """
    assert not validators.email("user@my_host.example.com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R8 — no leading or trailing hyphen in domain label
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_domain_label_leading_hyphen_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R8

    sub-domain = Let-dig [Ldh-str] requires the first character to be a
    letter or digit; a leading hyphen is not allowed.
    """
    assert not validators.email("user@-example.com")


def test_domain_label_trailing_hyphen_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R8

    Ldh-str ends with Let-dig, so a trailing hyphen is not allowed in a
    domain label.
    """
    assert not validators.email("user@example-.com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R13 — domain case insensitivity
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_domain_uppercase_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 2.4 — R13

    Domain names are case-insensitive per DNS rules; uppercase is valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("user@EXAMPLE.COM")


def test_domain_mixed_case_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 2.4 — R13

    Mixed-case domain names are valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("user@Example.Com")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R17 — domain must not be empty
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_empty_domain_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.4.1 — R17

    addr-spec = local-part "@" domain requires a non-empty domain.
    An address with a trailing '@' is invalid.
    """
    assert not validators.email("user@")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R9 — FQDN requirement / simple_host option
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_domain_without_dot_rejected_by_default():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 2.3.5 — R9

    On the public Internet only FQDNs (containing at least one dot) are
    valid. By default the validator should reject a single-label domain.
    """
    assert not validators.email("user@localhost")


def test_domain_without_dot_allowed_with_simple_host():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 2.3.5 — R9

    The simple_host option explicitly allows single-label domains for
    local/intranet use cases (validator docstring).
    """
    assert validators.email("user@localhost", simple_host=True)


def test_domain_two_labels_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 2.3.5 — R9

    A domain with at least two labels separated by a dot is a valid FQDN.
    """
    assert validators.email("user@example.com")


def test_domain_multiple_labels_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 2.3.5 — R9

    A domain with multiple dot-separated labels is valid.
    """
    assert validators.email("user@mail.example.co.uk")

"""Spec tests for email quoted-string local-part rules.

Rules covered: R6
Sources: RFC 5322 §3.2.4, §3.4.1 / RFC 5321 §4.1.2
"""

import validators


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R6 — quoted-string local-part
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_quoted_local_part_simple_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 — R6

    A quoted-string local-part enclosed in double-quotes is valid.
    """
    assert validators.email('"user"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_with_space_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 / RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R6

    Inside a quoted-string, a space (SP, %d32) is a valid qtextSMTP
    character and therefore valid in the local-part.
    """
    assert validators.email('"user name"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_with_special_chars_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 / RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R6

    Inside a quoted-string, characters such as '(),:;<>@' are allowed
    because the quoted form permits any printable ASCII character except
    unescaped '"' and '\'.
    """
    assert validators.email('"user@name"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_with_at_sign_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 / RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R6

    A quoted-string local-part containing an '@' sign is technically valid
    according to the RFC; the entire address still has exactly one
    structural '@' (the one separating local-part from domain).
    """
    assert validators.email('"user@name"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_empty_quoted_string_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 — R6

    quoted-string = DQUOTE *([FWS] qcontent) [FWS] DQUOTE  — zero
    qcontent characters is syntactically valid (empty quoted-string).
    """
    assert validators.email('""@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_unclosed_quote_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 — R6

    A local-part that starts with a double-quote but does not close it is
    not a valid quoted-string and must be rejected.
    """
    assert not validators.email('"user@example.com')


def test_local_part_bare_double_quote_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R6 / R15

    A bare double-quote that is not part of a properly delimited
    quoted-string is a 'special' and invalid in an unquoted local-part.
    """
    assert not validators.email('u"ser@example.com')

# Email Validation Rules

Extracted from RFC 5321 (SMTP) and RFC 5322 (Internet Message Format).

---

## R1 — Address structure: exactly one `@`
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`addr-spec = local-part "@" domain`  
A valid email address MUST contain exactly one `@` character separating the local-part from the domain.

## R2 — Local-part maximum length: 64 octets
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.1  
The maximum total length of a user name or other local-part is **64 octets**.

## R3 — Domain maximum length: 255 octets
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.5.3.1.2  
The maximum total length of a domain name or number is **255 octets**.

## R4 — Local-part dot-atom form: allowed characters
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3, §3.4.1  
`atext = ALPHA / DIGIT / "!" / "#" / "$" / "%" / "&" / "'" / "*" / "+" / "-" / "/" / "=" / "?" / "^" / "_" / "`" / "{" / "|" / "}" / "~"`  
`dot-atom-text = 1*atext *("." 1*atext)`  
In dot-atom form the local-part consists of `atext` characters optionally separated by dots. The characters `(`, `)`, `<`, `>`, `[`, `]`, `:`, `;`, `@`, `\`, `,`, and `"` (specials) are NOT allowed in the dot-atom form.

## R5 — Local-part dot rules: no leading, trailing, or consecutive dots
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3, §3.4.1  
`dot-atom-text = 1*atext *("." 1*atext)`  
In dot-atom form, the local-part must NOT begin with a dot, end with a dot, or contain consecutive dots (`..`).

## R6 — Local-part quoted-string form
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.4, §3.4.1 / RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
The local-part MAY be a quoted-string enclosed in double-quote characters (`"`). Inside the quoted string, any printable ASCII character (except `"` and `\`) is allowed without escaping; `"` and `\` must be escaped as `\"` and `\\`.  
RFC 5321 qtextSMTP: `%d32-33 / %d35-91 / %d93-126` (space and printable US-ASCII except `"` and `\`).

## R7 — Domain dot-atom form: sub-domain labels
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
`Domain = sub-domain *("." sub-domain)`  
`sub-domain = Let-dig [Ldh-str]`  
`Let-dig = ALPHA / DIGIT`  
`Ldh-str = *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" ) Let-dig`  
Each label must start with a letter or digit, end with a letter or digit, and contain only letters, digits, and hyphens. Underscores and other special characters are NOT permitted in domain labels.

## R8 — Domain label: no leading or trailing hyphen
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
`sub-domain = Let-dig [Ldh-str]` and `Ldh-str = *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "-" ) Let-dig`  
Domain labels MUST NOT begin or end with a hyphen.

## R9 — Domain: at least one dot for FQDN (internet mail)
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.3.5  
Only resolvable, fully-qualified domain names (FQDNs) are permitted in SMTP; a single-label domain (no dot) is not a valid FQDN on the public Internet (exception: the `simple_host` option relaxes this for local contexts).

## R10 — Domain literal: IPv4 address in brackets
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.3 / RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`address-literal = "[" ( IPv4-address-literal / IPv6-address-literal / General-address-literal ) "]"`  
When the domain part is an IP address literal it MUST be enclosed in square brackets `[...]`. For IPv4: `[d.d.d.d]` where each octet is 0–255.

## R11 — Domain literal: IPv6 address in brackets with `IPv6:` tag
**Source:** RFC 5321 §4.1.3  
`IPv6-address-literal = "IPv6:" IPv6-addr`  
IPv6 literals MUST use the `IPv6:` prefix inside brackets, e.g., `[IPv6:::1]`.

## R12 — Local-part case sensitivity
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.4  
The local-part of a mailbox MUST BE treated as case-sensitive by SMTP servers. (The validators library accepts both cases as syntactically valid.)

## R13 — Domain case insensitivity
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.4  
Mailbox domains follow normal DNS rules and are hence NOT case-sensitive.

## R14 — No bare `@` — both parts required
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1 / RFC 5321 §4.1.2  
Both the local-part and the domain part MUST be non-empty.

## R15 — Local-part specials not allowed outside quoted-string
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3  
`specials = "(" / ")" / "<" / ">" / "[" / "]" / ":" / ";" / "@" / "\" / "," / "." / DQUOTE`  
These characters appear in `specials` (not in `atext`) and MUST NOT appear in an unquoted local-part.

## R16 — Space not allowed in unquoted local-part
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3  
Whitespace (SP, HTAB) is not in `atext` and therefore MUST NOT appear in an unquoted local-part or outside CFWS context.

## R17 — Domain must not be empty
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`addr-spec = local-part "@" domain` requires a non-empty domain portion.

## R18 — Local-part must not be empty
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.4.1  
`local-part = dot-atom / quoted-string / obs-local-part` requires at least one character.

## R19 — atext characters are case-insensitive for matching
**Source:** RFC 5322 §3.2.3  
Both upper-case and lower-case letters are `ALPHA` and therefore valid atext. The local-part alphabet includes A–Z and a–z.

## R20 — Non-ASCII (high-bit) characters NOT permitted in standard SMTP
**Source:** RFC 5321 §2.4  
Systems MUST NOT define mailboxes that require non-ASCII characters (octets with the high-order bit set) in SMTP. The unextended SMTP service is 7-bit only.  
*(The validators library uses the `@validator` decorator and does accept certain extended Latin characters as an implementation extension; tests for that rely on the implementation docstring.)*

"""Spec tests for email domain part rules.

Rules covered: R3, R7, R8, R9, R13, R17

"""

import validators


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R3 — domain max 253/255 octets
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_domain_253_chars_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.5.3.1.2 — R3

    The maximum domain length is 255 octets per RFC 5321. The implementation
    checks <= 253 (consistent with DNS name constraints). A 253-character
    domain is valid.
    """
    # 63-char label + dot + 63-char label + dot + 63-char label + dot + 63-char TLD
    # = 63+1+63+1+63+1+61 = 253 chars total
    label_a = "a" * 63
    label_b = "b" * 63
    label_c = "c" * 63
    label_d = "d" * 61
    domain = f"{label_a}.{label_b}.{label_c}.{label_d}"
    assert len(domain) == 253
    assert validators.email(f"user@{domain}")


def test_domain_exceeds_253_chars_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5321 4.5.3.1.2 — R3

    A domain exceeding 253 characters is invalid.
    """
    # 254-character domain
    label = "a" * 63
    domain = f"{label}.{label}.{label}." + "b" * 62
    assert len(domain) == 254
    assert not validators.email(f"user@{domain}")

Rules covered: R6
Sources: RFC 5322 §3.2.4, §3.4.1 / RFC 5321 §4.1.2
"""

import validators


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# R6 — quoted-string local-part
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def test_quoted_local_part_simple_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 — R6

    A quoted-string local-part enclosed in double-quotes is valid.
    """
    assert validators.email('"user"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_with_space_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 / RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R6

    Inside a quoted-string, a space (SP, %d32) is a valid qtextSMTP
    character and therefore valid in the local-part.
    """
    assert validators.email('"user name"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_with_special_chars_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 / RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R6

    Inside a quoted-string, characters such as '(),:;<>@' are allowed
    because the quoted form permits any printable ASCII character except
    unescaped '"' and '\'.
    """
    assert validators.email('"user@name"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_with_at_sign_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 / RFC 5321 4.1.2 — R6

    A quoted-string local-part containing an '@' sign is technically valid
    according to the RFC; the entire address still has exactly one
    structural '@' (the one separating local-part from domain).
    """
    assert validators.email('"user@name"@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_empty_quoted_string_valid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 — R6

    quoted-string = DQUOTE *([FWS] qcontent) [FWS] DQUOTE  — zero
    qcontent characters is syntactically valid (empty quoted-string).
    """
    assert validators.email('""@example.com')


def test_quoted_local_part_unclosed_quote_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.4 — R6

    A local-part that starts with a double-quote but does not close it is
    not a valid quoted-string and must be rejected.
    """
    assert not validators.email('"user@example.com')


def test_local_part_bare_double_quote_invalid():
    """Spec: RFC 5322 3.2.3 — R6 / R15

    A bare double-quote that is not part of a properly delimited
    quoted-string is a 'special' and invalid in an unquoted local-part.
    """
    assert not validators.email('u"ser@example.com')
